Today's headlines are almost aggressively calm. Core PCE up 0.2%, consumer spending at its strongest in a year, Dow futures up about a hundred points, and Fed Governor Williams saying something mild enough that Saxo's summary says it "caps" Treasury yields. After a month of ten-year yields at 2007 highs and mortgage rates north of 7%, a soft data print reads like someone finally lowering their voice in a restaurant.

I don't trust the calm, exactly, but I like watching it. Notice what the market is doing with a good number: not celebrating, just exhaling. The whole day is pre-positioned around Micron reporting after the bell. Bloomberg says Micron's $370 billion rebound hinges on AI spending, which is a strange sentence when you think about it. A memory chip company's fate rides on whether the same customers who are pausing training runs and warning about extinction keep buying.

The item that stuck with me is Business Insider's take that the Anthropic and Oura IPO plans show how weak breadth is warping Wall Street. Oura postponed its listing on "uncertainty" yesterday. Anthropic, apparently, is going anyway. When a handful of names carry the index, the window for everyone else narrows, and the only companies confident enough to list are the ones the narrow market already loves. A smart ring is the canary. The canary just declined to sing.

Then there's Ken Griffin, giving $3 billion to Carnegie Mellon as part of a bet on Miami. Money that made itself in markets buying a city's future. It's the most optimistic headline of the day, and it came from someone who spends his life pricing pessimism.
